The Two Ingredients an Ensemble Needs:
content:
\textbf{The Two Ingredients an Ensemble Needs:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item \textbf{Accuracy:} each base learner must individually beat random guessing (Examples 5.4 to 5.6 show the ensemble amplifies whatever the base learners already have — good or bad)
\item \textbf{Diversity:} the base learners should make \textbf{different} mistakes; if every base learner is wrong on exactly the same examples, majority vote gives no benefit at all, since diversity is what allows correct learners to outvote a mistaken one
\item The next two sections cover two different strategies for building a diverse committee of base learners: \textbf{Bagging} (Section 5.2) trains learners in parallel on different random samples of the data, and \textbf{Boosting} (Section 5.3) trains learners in sequence, each one focusing on the previous learner's mistakes
\end{enumerate}

\newpage

title: Bootstrap Sample
content:
A bootstrap sample is formed by drawing $n$ examples \textbf{with replacement} from an original training set of size $n$. Because the same example can be picked more than once, a bootstrap sample usually contains repeated examples and leaves some original examples out entirely, even though its total size still equals $n$.

This is the same "draw, note it down, put it back, draw again" idea as drawing a card from a deck, recording it, and returning it before the next draw.

Bagging
Bagging Algorithm
content:
\textbf{Input:} training set of $n$ examples, number of bootstrap samples $B$, a base learning algorithm

\textbf{Output:} $B$ trained models and a combined prediction rule

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item For $b=1$ to $B$: draw a bootstrap sample $S_b$ of size $n$, with replacement, from the training set.
\item Train a base learner $M_b$ using only $S_b$.
\item Repeat steps 1 to 2 until all $B$ models are trained.
\item For a new test point, obtain a prediction from every model $M_1,\ldots,M_B$.
\item Combine the $B$ predictions by majority vote (classification) or by averaging (regression).
\item Return the combined prediction.
\end{enumerate}

Why Bagging Helps: enumerate[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt] Each bootstrap
content:
\textbf{Why Bagging Helps:}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Each bootstrap sample is slightly different, so the $B$ trained models make \textbf{different} mistakes — the diversity condition from Section 5.1.2
\item Bagging works best with \textbf{unstable, high-variance} base learners such as deep, unpruned decision trees, since small changes in the training set noticeably change such a tree
\item \textbf{Random Forest} is bagging applied to decision trees, with one extra twist: at each split, only a random subset of attributes is even considered, which further increases diversity between the trees
\end{enumerate}

title: Boosting
Example Weight Update
content: Every training example starts with equal weight $w_i = \frac{1}{n}$. After each base learner $M_t$ is trained, examples it \textbf{misclassified} have their weight \textbf{increased}, and examples it classified \textbf{correctly} have their weight \textbf{decreased} (or left relatively smaller after renormalizing), so the next learner is forced to focus more on the hard, previously misclassified examples.

title: Model (Voting) Weight
content:
Each trained base learner $M_t$ is given a voting weight $\alpha_t$ based on its (weighted) error rate $\epsilon_t$ on the data it was trained on:
\[
\alpha_t = \frac{1}{2}\ln\left(\frac{1-\epsilon_t}{\epsilon_t}\right)
\]
A lower error rate $\epsilon_t$ produces a \textbf{larger} $\alpha_t$, meaning a more accurate base learner gets more say in the final weighted vote.

This mirrors the ensemble-accuracy calculations of Section 5.1.2: a base learner that is far better than random guessing ($\epsilon_t$ close to $0$) deserves much more influence than one that is barely better than a coin flip ($\epsilon_t$ close to $0.5$).

title: Boosting Algorithm (AdaBoost-Style)
content:
\textbf{Input:} training set of $n$ examples, number of rounds $T$, a base learning algorithm

\textbf{Output:} $T$ trained models $M_1,\ldots,M_T$ with voting weights $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_T$

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em,itemsep=4pt]
\item Initialize every example's weight to $w_i = \dfrac{1}{n}$.
\item For $t=1$ to $T$: train base learner $M_t$ on the training set using the current example weights.
\item Compute $M_t$'s weighted error rate $\epsilon_t$ (the total weight of the examples it misclassified).
\item Compute the model's voting weight $\alpha_t = \dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{1-\epsilon_t}{\epsilon_t}\right)$.
\item Increase the weight of every example $M_t$ misclassified, and decrease the weight of every example it classified correctly; then renormalize all weights to sum to $1$.
\item Repeat steps 2 to 5 for all $T$ rounds.
\item For a new test point, combine all $T$ predictions using a weighted vote: $\displaystyle\sum_t \alpha_t \cdot [\text{prediction of } M_t]$.
\item Return the combined prediction.
\end{enumerate}

Three trained classifiers predict a new example's class as: Yes, No, Yes. Combine these predictions using majority vote.

title: Practice Problem 1
content:
Five regression models predict a car's price (lakhs) as: 12, 14, 13, 15, 11. Combine these predictions using averaging.

\item

title: Practice Problem 2
content:
Explain in 2 to 3 lines why an ensemble of classifiers, each with individual accuracy below 50\%, can end up performing worse than any single classifier.

\item

title: Practice Problem 3
content:
Three independent classifiers each have accuracy $p=0.8$. Compute the accuracy of the majority-vote ensemble (correct when all 3, or exactly 2 of 3, are correct).

\item

title: Practice Problem 4
content:
Three independent classifiers each have accuracy $p=0.5$. Compute the accuracy of the majority-vote ensemble, and explain what this result shows about the accuracy condition needed for ensembles to help.

\item

title: Practice Problem 5
content:
An original training set has 6 examples $Y_1,\ldots,Y_6$. A bootstrap sample drawn is: $Y_2,Y_5,Y_2,Y_2,Y_6,Y_5$. List which examples are repeated and which are left out (out-of-bag).

\item

title: Practice Problem 6
content:
For an original training set of size $n=6$, drawn 6 times with replacement to build one bootstrap sample, compute the probability that a specific example $Y_1$ is never selected.

\item

title: Practice Problem 7
content:

title: Practice Problem 8
content:

title: Practice Problem 9
content:

title: Practice Problem 10
content:

title: Practice Problem 11
content:

title: Practice Problem 12
content:
Four boosted learners predict a new example's class with the following (prediction, voting weight) pairs: $(+1, 0.6)$, $(-1, 0.9)$, $(+1, 0.4)$, $(-1, 0.3)$. Compute the final weighted-vote prediction.

title: Practice Problem 13
content:
Three training examples start with equal weight $w_i=\frac{1}{3}$. A base learner misclassifies only $X_2$. If the misclassified example's weight is tripled and the correctly classified examples' weights are left unchanged, find the renormalized weights for all three examples.
